newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak opposition says referendum petition success.
newsitem.headline: Slovak opposition says referendum petition success.

text.p: Slovakia's opposition said on Tuesday it had collected more than 350,000 signatures needed to force a referendum on the direct election of the President.

"We prefer not to state the exact number (of signatures) before they have been checked, but...we can say the petition has been successful," Ivan Simko, vice-chairman of the opposition Christian Democratic Movement (KDH) who heads the petition committee, told journalists.
Under Slovak law, if a petition has 350,000 signatures, the president must call a referendum on the subject within 90 days.

The referendum is aimed at preventing Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar from assuming presidential powers before the election of a new president in March 1998, some six months before the next general elections.

The ruling coalition, headed by Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), and the opposition appear unable to agree on a common presidential candidate. Neither is able to garner the three-fifths majority necessary in the 150-seat house to push through their own choice.
If a stalemate occurs, Meciar, an avowed political foe of President Michal Kovac, would assume presidential powers. He has rejected the referendum and called for a voter boycott.
At least 50 percent of the electorate must vote in a referendum to make it valid, and a simple majority of voters would be needed approve a change to the constitution.

Simko said the petitioners would like to combine the referendum on presidential elections with another referendum, on the country's possible membership in NATO, which was initiated by HZDS and approved by parliament last Friday.
"We would welcome if both the referenda were held at the same time," he said. "It would at least save money." The final decision on dates for both is up to the president.
The same date for both would be politically significant because most of opposition and petition supporters also favour of NATO membership, according to recent opinion polls.
"It would be a chance for Slovakia to take a significant step either upwards or downwards on the path to democracy," Jan Budaj, vice-chairman of the Democratic Union (DU) said.

Some political analysts say the referendum might also be a dress rehearsal for opposition parties heading into a 1998 general election because the petition has united all opposition parties, except for the Party of the Democratic Left (SDL), the reformed communists.
"This action can help us create a strong alternative to the current ruling power," Laszlo Gyurovsky of the Hungarian Civic Party (MOS) said.
